utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Dr. Allsop.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up the document which has just been mentioned by Mr. Robinson, 1D06102.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Allsop, do you see the document before you? Is this your CV which you have kindly brought us?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you kindly tell the Trial Chamber something about your education and about your career path as well as about your educational background. First of all, tell us something about your education.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I started my formal education as a mechanical engineer at the age of 16. I actually served an apprenticeship as a craft engineer, and I then went to evening class. I did well at evening classes and they moved me to -- into the next level of apprenticeship. I continued my education at that technical college, gaining an ordinary national certificate, then a higher national certificate, in mechanical engineering. I then went on to take a college diploma, which is the level of a first degree, bachelor's degree. This gave me the academic exemption to become a chartered engineer. I then studied for a master's degree in thermodynamics and fluid mechanics at the City University in London. This was followed by a period of research at the British Non-Ferrous Metals Research Association, where I registered my research for a Ph.D. in thermodynamics and fluid mechanics. In 1989 I was then elected a fellow at the Institute of Mechanical Engineers. So my current career in the area of weapons systems began in 1987, 25 years ago, when I joined what was then the Royal Military College of Science, and in 1984 the Royal Military College of Science was actually privatised so that that meant that the teaching that the normally being carried out by civilian staff, then that teaching was taken on by Cranfield University. So when I joined the Royal Military College of Science, I joined as a member of staff of Cranfield University, and I joined there as an assistant director of the weapons systems assessment and technical support unit, where we supplied technical advice and technical support to the Ministry of Defence on matters concerning small and medium calibre weapons systems. After a number of years in that department, I soon moved over and became a member of the lecturing staff, and so I took on the responsibility for teaching at the undergraduate level, post-graduate level, and the supervision of PhD students in research. And the areas that I specialised in, again for small/medium-calibre weapons, basically weapons which are man-portable, and their weapon design, ammunition design, and their ballistics. I actually retired four weeks ago from Cranfield university. So my CV tells you that I am a member of staff at Cranfield University. I'm not. I actually retired from there four weeks ago. I was when the CV was presented. I still lecture there and also provide advice on technical matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Allsop. Is it correct that, inter alia, during your career you yourself gained knowledge in forensic ballistics, as it is stated on page 1, and that that was accepted at the university and that you also lectured in that area?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes. In -- it would be 15 years ago, then the Cranfield University started a course in forensic engineering and science, and I was asked to provide the lecturing content on that course on the -- those aspects regarding fire-arms and ballistics. Then five years ago then that course was considerably expanded and so we actually started a number of M.Sc. courses in forensics, one of which was specifically forensic ballistics. I was responsible for the academic input to that and so that I taught and researched in the subject of forensic ballistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it also correct that on page 1 there begins a list of your papers and areas that you were involved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Allsop, you have also authored three books. For two of them you were the team leader with co-authors and the third was authored by you yourself, and we can see all of them under the title "books written." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: That is correct. I wrote these textbooks which are actually used by the Cranfield University as the course books on our masters degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, may I tender this CV into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Next Defence exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, 65 ter number 1D06102 will be Exhibit D2369.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And now I would like to call up 1D05015. This is Dr. Allsop's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting, Dr. Allsop, while you were studying all those weapons, did you also learn about the 120-millimetre mortar?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: The 120-millimetre mortar is not actually a weapon I did work on, although I did study it as part of gaining knowledge on mortar systems, then I only studied it from the point of view of its design and the design of its ammunition. At the college where I work, then we have a very extensive weapons collection and a very extensive ammunition collection, and we have a 120-millimetre mortar in our weapons collection and we have the ammunition in our weapons collection as well. The actual mortar and the ammunition are not the same as the one which was actually used in this particular incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When it comes to ballistics principles, i.e., the aerodynamic ballistic principles, are you familiar with those also for the 120-millimetre mortar system?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I am. The actual principles are not really dependent upon the calibre. We use exactly the same laws of physics and the same laws of thermodynamics and fluid mechanics as we would for any mortar system. And in fact, I actually designed our own 60-millimetre spigot mortar firing an inert projectile which we actually take out onto our explosive range and we fire it, and we use that to demonstrate the principles of mortar ballistics to our students, and we actually get them to write up an assignment that I set for them based upon those firings so that they can actually predict the performance, the theoretical performance, and then they go out and they test the mortar and they see how their predictions stand up to the practical results.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you asked to provide your opinion as to whether one can determine the distance from which the 120-millimetre mortar was fired at the Markale Market in 1994?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I was asked to do that and I actually undertook the study and produced a report on my findings and on -- based upon the information that was submitted to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the gist of that task to demonstrate whether based on what penetrated into the ground one could determine the distance from which the shell was fired?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: That is correct. The -- the gist of what I was asked to do was to say if it was possible from the tail fin of the mortar embedded in the ground, whether it was possible to predict the impact velocity of the mortar and also the impact angle of the mortar, with a view to predicting back to see how -- where the mortar may have been fired from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was your opinion?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: My opinion was that from that information alone, from the information given from the tail fin embedded in the asphalt, that it was not possible to predict either the impact velocity or the impact angle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With this regard I would kindly ask you to look at your report together with us to see how you arrived at that conclusion. Can you tell the Trial Chamber from bullet point 2.1 about the impact centre which has to be behind the gravitation centre while the mortar is flying. Can you try and explain the Trial Chamber the importance of that.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: When we fire projectiles, then in order to maximise their performance then they are normally much longer -- the dimension in their length is greater than the dimension in their diameter, so that that means this gives us all sorts of advantages. It reduces the aerodynamic drag, it allows us to maximise the payload for a particular calibre, but it does introduce problems of stability. What we need to do is to ensure that the projectile is stable; in other words, we have to ensure that the axis of the projectile is always aligned with its trajectory. In order to do that, we have to have some form of actually stabilising the projectile. With mortars, for various reasons which I can go into if you wish, but with mortars then we fin stabilise them. What this means is that we have a stabilising boom which is attached to the back of the bomb, and the purpose of this is to ensure that the centre of pressure acting upon the mortar while it's in flight is actually behind the centre of gravity. The reason for this is that if we have any perturbance, and we do have a number of perturbances to our projectiles when we fire them, when we launch them, for instance, then we have a perturbance because as the projectile leaves the end of the barrel then the gases flow around the back of it and it's actually in a field of reverse flow, and of course it's not designed to fly in a field of reverse flow. So it tries to stabilise itself flying in that direction. Luckily this only lasts for a short period of time, but it does introduce yaw to -- the projectile starts to try and swing around and so it introduces yaw. Now if the centre of pressure is actually in front of the centre of gravity, then that yaw will increase; if it's behind, then it will decrease. Because basically what's happening is that you have a positive overturning moment when the centre of pressure is in front of the centre of gravity and so that that means that it will actually try to rotate by the centre of gravity. When it's behind it, it will do the exact opposite, it would try and step back into the -- to be in line with the axis, so the axis is in line with the trajectory. Unfortunately, what it does it overcorrects and so that now we have yaw in the other direction, and so we have a series of oscillations during -- during that period which are then dampen-type and then the projectile after a time or a certain time will fly in a reasonably stable condition. So our projectiles are therefore designed to be actually self-stabilising.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have mentioned that it is lucky that it doesn't last long. When it comes to those oscillations, are they higher in longer shell trajectories?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: It's all dependent upon the distance between the centre of gravity and the centre of pressure. And so typically we like to actually have one calibre's distance between the centre of pressure and the centre of gravity. For instance, with a 120-millimetre, then we try to make the centre of pressure about 120 millimetres back from that. If it's close -- if it's actually less than that, then the oscillations tend to be greater because the correcting couple is too -- is actually quite large. If we make it any greater than that so it's a very stable projectile, then we end up with a very long tail -- tail boom, tail fin, which adds to the weight, adds to the cost, and so on. So we look for a compromise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In that sense, whether conditions and other physical conditions, are they important when it comes to the updating of the system, and why are meteorological and other conditions important?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: The weather conditions can have some considerable effect upon the trajectory of the projectile. The obvious ones that you are probably aware of are that the wind -- if we have a tail wind so that the wind is blowing in the same direction, then the projectile will travel farther, if we have one blowing towards you, it will travel less far. If it's firing -- if it's -- the wind is blowing from left, it will actually push the projectile to the right and vice versa. Those are the obvious ones, but there are other conditions as well. One is the temperature itself. These projectiles, they're launched by burning a propellant in -- basically in the tube, the mortar itself, and the burning rate of the propellant, and therefore the pressures which you develop and therefore the velocity at which the projectile is launched is affected by the temperature, so that the higher the temperature then the greater will be the muzzle velocity of the mortar. And typically -- I'm used to doing tests and trials for NATO, and the NATO requirement is that we must know what the effect of conditions from minus 40 to plus 70 degrees centigrade. And as an example, we normally design our projectiles and our charges to operate at ambient conditions, which is about 21 degrees centigrade. If you actually increase the temperature up to 70 degrees centigrade -- 70 degrees centigrade is a high temperature. You wouldn't expect the actual air temperature to be 70 degrees, but under certain conditions when you store the ammunition, then the direct sunlight on the storage system can actually increase the temperature of the munition up to 70 degrees centigrade. What that does, that actually increases the muzzle velocity by 10 per cent. That gives you some idea of the effect that temperature has on our charge system. In addition to that, then the aerodynamic drag on any projectile is dependent upon the actual pressure of the air, the density of the air, and so that the aerodynamic drag is less, with less dense air, and is greater with more dense air. But to put this into context, then mortars are slow-moving projectiles compared to other munitions. They are typically subsonic, they typically operate maximum velocity about 300 metres per second. Artillery will actually be working at three times that velocity. And as aerodynamic drag is a function of velocity squared, you can see that the actual drag forces on mortars is not very high so that in other words these other conditions, these conditions that affect the drag coefficient, the drag characteristics of the mortar, are actually less affected than they are on other munitions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I hope the interpreter will have time. We don't have the interpretation in Serbian. In chapter 2 you said that the tubes in the case of indirect weapons could fire between temperatures of 45 and 85 degrees. What would happen if one fired at a temperature of 40 or 89 degrees, for example, from these barrels?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I think you mean angles, not temperature. So I will answer my question -- your question assuming that I'm talking about angles rather than temperature, degrees in angle rather than degrees in temperature. The -- a mortar is a very simple system, and the -- they fire very heavy projectiles for their size and their weight. That means the recoil is very, very, very, very great. It gives you some idea then the 81-millimetre mortars I normally work on on full charge, then the recoil force is 45 tonnes, and so that you can see that the only way we can manage that, those sort of forces, is by directing the recoil force directly into the ground. And we do this via a base plate. We actually mount the mortar on the base plate so that our minimum angle is set because of these very high forces and so that our -- when we -- when we are firing at 45 degrees, that gives us our maximum angle -- that gives us typically our maximum distance, not maximum angle. And so that if we wanted to fire at 40 degrees, for instance, then it would go less far and it would go actually about the same distance as if we were firing at 50 degrees. So we reach a stage where firing at lower angles reduces the range. If we start off at high angle, as we reduce that angle, the range increases until we get to about 45 degrees, and after that it starts decreasing it. So there is no advantage in going to 40 degrees so far as the range is concerned. The disadvantage is that what's happening is that we're getting an increasingly large component of recoil parallel to the ground, and so that that will then start pushing the base -- the base plate along the ground rather than into the ground. So this is why we restrict our minimum angle to 45 degrees. When it comes to firing at higher angles, we normally limit it to 85 degrees for a number of reasons. The maximum range of a mortar -- supposing we have the maximum range of a mortar is say 6 kilometres. The minimum range going from 45 to 89 actually reduces that to about one-third, so that it's going from 6 kilometres at 45 degrees, as we elevate it to 85 degrees it will reduce that to approximately, this is only approximately figures, to about 2 kilometres. The problem is that when we get to these high angles, then a small -- a small variation in angle has a large effect upon its range at these very short ranges. And so that the projectile's in the air for a very long time, so that if we have a wind blowing, for instance, especially if it's blowing from in front of you, it can actually blow the projectile back so that it will actually fall on top of you, which is -- which would be inconvenient. But the main reason is that it's because of this sensitivity in the range increments for small changes in the angle itself. And so the way that we actually reduce the -- go to shorter ranges is by actually reducing the velocity by going to different charge system.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. As for the forces acting in a direction contrary to the direction in which the shell is fired, do these forces leave any traces on the ground; and if so, what sort of form do these traces take -- or rather, I don't mean the point of impact. I mean the point from which the shell was actually fired.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: It's extremely important that the mortar is actually mounted on a very solid base. That's one of the problems that is encountered when using mortars, and quite often it's necessary to actually bed the mortar in. The UK procedure normally is that bedding -- the bedding procedure can take up to six shots. Each time the mortar is actually fired, then if it's not bedded incorrectly, then the mortar will actually move during firing. And so typically it will actually bed itself in, and the angle will actually increase slightly and it will actually fall short and so that although you've set it up to fire at one particular angle, then it's actually launching at a slightly different angle. And so consequently it's important, therefore, that you actually bed the actual base plate in on to a very firm footing. And so that if it was soft ground, for instance, then the mortar can actually end up by driving the base plate to a substantial depth into the ground. It is a major problem and it's particularly a problem in snow, and I have a colleague that -- who actually designed as a whole system whereby that certain bags are used to spread the load as wide as possible so that they can actually be fired -- the mortars can actually be fired in the snow. But on soft ground then it is a problem, and you will leave a -- quite a large imprint of the base plate in the ground. But you try to avoid that situation. You try to find somewhere where, in fact, it will be on a more solid ground. For instance, if you were firing on concrete, asphalt, and so on, you may on asphalt, because asphalt is quite soft, then you may leave the impression of the underneath of the base plate. The base plate typically has some projections on them so that they actually grip the surface because you still get the component of force acting parallel to the ground at 45 degrees, so it will still slide forward unless you actually have something to stop them driving themselves backwards. This is why you typically underneath the base plate, then do you have sort of protrusions which actually try to prevent from doing that. So you may see the mark of those protrusions on some surfaces. On concrete, then, you probably wouldn't see that -- see those marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a look at the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In chapter 3 of your report you speak about predicting distances, assessing distances. Could you tell us what has to be done in order to determine the distance from which a shell was fired at the site of impact or on the basis of the site of impact.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: If we want to predict where a projectile was fired from, from the evidence at the impact site, then what we need to know is the impact velocity and the impact angle. And so that we could then work backwards from trajectory calculations or range tables, the position from where the shell was fired from. But those are the two -- those are the two characteristics that we need to know. The other thing of course that we need to know is all of those -- it depends how accurately you need to know this. For instance, your calculations when you predict backwards, then they will probably be based initially on ambient conditions, still air. You really need to know for reasonable accuracy the temperature so that you can do any temperature corrections for the charge. It would be an advantage to know the wind conditions at the time, the height of the mortar relative to the impact site, whether it was above, below, or at the same level, because they will all affect the range. But providing you know these and providing you have information on these, then you can, in fact, project back from the point of impact to the point of launch just using those two values. And in fact, manufacturers, when they produce their range tables, then what they have to do is that they produce their range tables for ambient conditions and for a number of different charges and so on. But of course if we actually need to provide information so that we can actually correct for such things as charge temperatures and so on, then we cannot fire vast numbers of bombs in order to find that information. Then typically what we do is that we will actually predict using computer programmes what the effect will be. We have to validate those and so that we actually measure the impact velocity and the impact angles and so that we can then compare them with our predictions. That's part of the validation process.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When it comes to accuracy and the precision, which element is the most important one. What is the significance of the angle of impact for the precision with which one can determine the angle, and how do these variations affect the site from which the shell was fired?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: If we consider the trajectory of a mortar, then if we launched it at 45 degrees, its maximum angle, then if there was no aerodynamic drag then the impact angle -- if of course the impact -- the launch site and the impact site were on the same level, then it would actually impact at the same angle. We've got aerodynamic drag which is actually slowing the projectile throughout its trajectory, so that means it will typically impact, again in rough figures, about 5 degrees steeper angle than this. And the -- interestingly, the steeper the angle of the impact, then the -- this means that the steeper will be the impact at launch. But as I've already said, when it comes to the sensitivity of range with angle, it's more sensitive at the high angles than it is at the low angles, so that - in other words - if you were trying to predict to a reasonable degree of accuracy the range at which the bomb was launched and the impact angle was a low angle, then your predictions would be actually more accurate than if they were a high angle purely because very small variations in angle at high elevation have a greater effect on range.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In item 3 you say that when one predicts where the shell was launched from, one does that on the basis of the impact velocity. How is the impact velocity determined? In fact, how does one assess that impact velocity?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: If we were producing range tables, then of course what we would do is we would actually measure the impact velocity using a Doppler radar. But in the case that we are talking about here, then if we want to calculate what the impact velocity is -- if we want to calculate what that is from the evidence of -- at the actual site of the impact of the bomb, then that's extremely difficult to do. It depends upon the sort of evidence that there is at the impact site. In the case that we have here, then the evidence was the stabilising fin buried in the ground. That essentially is the only information from which we can try to calculate what the impact velocity was, and so that the tail fin is ejected from the bomb upon impact. Upon impact what happens is that the fuse will initiate the detonator. We will get a detonation wave which runs from the front of the bomb through to the rear. And as this detonation wave travels through the explosive, it will actually start breaking up the shell body, and then the gases behind it will eject the broken components side as fragments. When it gets to the rear of the bomb then we will again -- we will get exactly the same thing happening and the ejection -- the tail fin will be ejected back in the opposite direction from where it was -- along the -- in the opposite direction from which it impacted. So if we know what the velocity the tail boom is ejected from the back from the bomb, then that can give us some information on what the impact velocity of the bomb may have been. For example, if the impact velocity of the bomb was, say, 200 metres per second, and the ejection velocity of the tail fin was 200 metres per second, then we would expect that the tail fin would almost stop; and therefore, we actually find it very, very close to the impact site. If, in fact, the ejection velocity of the tail fin was, for instance, 150 metres per second, it means that we would get a net rearward velocity of 50 metres per second. To put this into context, 50 metres per second doesn't sound very fast, but we can actually calculate approximately how far that will actually travel at 45 degrees, for instance, its maximum angle. It's a very, very simple equation. It's just that the range equals the velocity squared divided by G, the acceleration due to gravity. So it's 30 metres per second, for instance, 30 metres per second squared is -- 30 times 30 is 900 divided by our acceleration due to gravity, which is approximately 10 - 9.81 - so you see it will be ejected backwards by about 90 metres, to about 90 metres. If, in fact, it's the other way around so that -- so that, in fact -- I've got that -- I'm sorry, can I just read what I said. I think I might be saying this the wrong way around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can read the transcript if you like.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's just one so I -- I -- suddenly --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see page 3 in the e-court system, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just want to make sure I'm -- I must admit I'm more nervous than I'd like to admit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no. I would ask nobody speak from now on. Doctor, you can read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. No, in fact, if we have the mortar bomb coming in at 200 metres per second, the ejection velocity is 150 metres per second, it will carry on at 50 metres per second. If the ejection velocity was 250 metres per second, the tail fin is ejected by -- at 250 metres per second, it would actually be ejected rearwards at a velocity of 50 metres per second. And so that if we -- you see, I then said 30 metres per second -- and so there's 50 metres per second - 50 metres per second - 50 times 50 is 2.500, so divided by 10, 250 metres. So at 50 metres per second it will actually be ejected back by 250 metres.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would be grateful if Mr. Allsop could slow down for the benefit of the interpreters in the B/C/S booth I thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I talk fast the more nervous I get, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, could you now tell us whether we have understood this correctly. After the explosion, two extremes of the shell behave differently in terms of velocity. At one end we have an acceleration and at the other end, that part in fact slows down. Which end is subject to acceleration and which end slows down, decelerates?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I think you're referring to the fuse and the tail fin so that, in fact, if the -- what will happen is that when the bomb detonates, then the fuse will be ejected forward, so that means the velocity will actually be added to the impact velocity. So if it's ejected forward at a hundred metres per second, it impacts at 200 metres per second, then it will actually be ejected forward at 300 metres per second; whereas, if the bomb impacts and we consider the ejection velocity of the tail fin, the ejection velocity of the tail fin is subtracted from the -- from the forward part -- velocity of the bomb. So in one case we add the ejection velocity to the impact velocity, in the other case we subtract it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Allsop, just putting it for myself in as simple term as possible: The faster the mortar bomb is falling, i.e., the greater the altitude that the projectile reached before it starts to fall back to earth, the more likely it is that the tail boom will be found embedded in the ground rather than ejected behind the bomb by any distance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: So really, when you find a tail fin assembly embedded in the ground the -- from a layman's point of view, the -- it is likely that the mortar has fallen a considerable distance and therefore obtained a high terminal velocity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That really depends upon the ejection velocity of the tail fin. If the ejection velocity of the tail fin is very low, for instance, on our 81-millimetre mortar, then the tail fin ejection velocity appears to be very low, and so consequently it's always ejected away from the site. It's very rare that we actually find a tail fin anywhere near the site with our 81-millimetre mortars. So under those conditions and then for that particular munition, then we cannot say that. But for a system whereby the ejection velocity is higher, then you're correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: And I don't want to confuse anyone else, and I certainly don't want to confuse myself. When the fuse is ejected forward, the resultant force going backwards, that must also assist in ejecting the tail boom in the opposite direction to the travel or am I making an elementary physics mistake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think you're making an elementary physics mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, that's why I wanted to check. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, do you need -- do you feel the need to go on talking about that or shall we move on to something else?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I would like to say something about the ejection velocity of the tail boom. I know of no method that can actually accurately predict this, so there we actually have a problem. The only way that we can really get data on the ejection velocity of the tail boom is from actually carrying out trials and actually measuring them. The fragmentation process is a very, very complex process, and we have some techniques which have stood as reasonable stead over the years which can actually predict the ejection velocity of fragments from very simple geometries, but the tail boom is not a simple geometry. It's a very complex geometry. These prediction techniques, then they have severe restrictions, and to try and apply these methods to calculating that ejection velocity is fraught with hazard. I know of no way that you can actually do this and get an answer which is anywhere near the correct one. There is another thing which we have to consider, and that is the question of dispersion, the dispersion of results. And when we talk about the range of a mortar, then we talk about the mean range. So suppose we talk about the maximum range of a mortar being 6 kilometres, then typically the dispersion of a mortar in terms of its projectiles about the point of impact is about 1 per cent of its range. In azimuth it's about half a per cent. So in other words, the impact at 6 kilometres, that will have a variation of 1 per cent, 60 metres forward, 60 metres backwards. So in other words, we could expect normally that it would actually fall between those two points, between 660 metres and 6.060 metres and 5.940 metres. But when we talk of dispersions, then what we're talking about are standard deviations, and so that one standard deviation actually equates to a 68 per cent probability that they will actually -- that that will actually occur, so that when we talk about measuring, for instance, the ejection velocity of our tail boom, and we do that experimentally, then there will be variations on a round-to-round basis. So that supposing we fired a hundred rounds, then we would fire -- we can actually calculate what the mean would be. We can also calculate the standard deviation. What that will tell us is what the variation in that ejection velocity is. So when we talk about a mortar having an ejection velocity of plus or minus 20 metres per second, then what this can only mean is that it actually has a standard deviation of 20 metres per second, so that supposing that the ejection velocity was 600 -- 200 metres per second, plus or minus 10 metres per second, then it means that -- it does not mean that 100 per cent of the tail booms would actually be ejected backwards between the velocities of 190 and 210; it means 68 per cent of them will be. And so that we have to take into account that when we do any calculation on what the ejection velocity will be, then we can calculate the mean -- if we had a method we would calculate the mean - I don't think we have a method where we can calculate the mean - but we cannot calculate what the standard deviation would be. We can only measure that from experimental results.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we move on to page 4, I would like to ask you about velocities. The fuse tunnel, can it be the stabiliser if the fuse disperses and remains on the surface? Can a fuse tunnel be anything else but a fuse? Can it produce anything else but a fuse?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: By that I think you're asking that if the tail fin does not travel forward and strike the ground in the area of the -- where the fuse is actually pushed into the ground, if that does not happen, is there anything else that could be ejected forward to enter the impact crater made by the fuse. I can't see that there would be anything else that would actually -- could actually be buried along with the fuse. The only thing that could happen is that -- you will have a fuse tunnel, you would have a hole in which the fuse is actually pushed into the ground, and then -- it would -- almost certainly what would happen is that the loose soil would then collapse and would also fill -- tend to fill that hole, and it really depends upon the cohesive strength of the ground in which indeed that's actually buried as to what extent that would actually happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Why do we refer to that thing, a fuse tunnel? Can any other part of the shell do the same if a fuse tunnel did not create a tunnel? If I told you that the fuse was not embedded, that it was dispersed and it remained on the ground, and we found the stabiliser 25 centimetres embedded in the ground, how would you interpret that? What would you make of that?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: If for some reason the fuse completely disintegrated and was dispersed somehow sideways so that it did not -- so that no part actually impacted directly in front of it, then -- and if the stabilising boom was actually found in the ground, it can only be because the forward velocity of the stabiliser boom at impact was actually greater than its ejection velocity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How often would that occur?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: We would know -- have to know what the impact velocities were and we would have to compare them with the known ejection velocities. At the moment we know what the impact velocity will be. Typically, the impact velocities will be slightly less on level -- providing we're talking here of the launch height being the same as the impact height. Then the impact velocity will be slightly less than the launch velocity. So we have a knowledge of that. What we don't have is a knowledge of the true ejection velocity. So afraid I'm not able to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm particularly interested about deviation. You have noticed yourself that the damage on the connection between the stabiliser boom and the body of the bomb is -- that that damage is asymmetrical. Just a while ago you were talking about deviation or - if I may put it that way - meandering of the bomb in flight. Can that meandering also appear in the ground itself? How do you account for the asymmetrical nature of the damage?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: The front of the damage done stabiliser boom, you could see in figure 2 that it's clearly a point of almost 45 degrees. This indicates it's actually failed in shear as opposed to in compressional tension, which has no specific meaning. But the fact that it's not on the axis indicates that there's some asymmetry in the system, and I've given that some considerable thought as to what that could be and why that's actually happened, and we -- the immediate reaction would be that what we have is we have an asymmetric pressure which is acting on the inside of the bomb itself, so how could that occur? If the inside of the bomb was symmetric, then we would expect the force from the pressure to be symmetric as well, and therefore the failure to be symmetric and therefore the point to be on the central line of the axis. It may be that the -- that the inside of the bomb was not, in fact, symmetric. The -- in my -- the early part of my report then I said that the bomb body, for instance, was made of a casting. Now, this is what the -- this is what the literature that I reviewed told me, but in fact I since learnt that that may well have -- would probably have been not from a casting but from a forging. A casting is not made very accurately, so if it had have been a casting, that would -- could have been one of the reasons why that occurred, because castings are not usually used because they cannot be made sufficiently accurate. Also, their mechanical properties aren't good enough. But it would appear that subsequent to my review of the literature I found that it's almost certainly actually a forging, so that probably rules that out. There could be another reason and that is that these shell bodies, they fragment naturally, so that in other words we have a smooth surface and we have this detonation wave running up there and so that we get a whole variety of fragments, large, small, some are too large and some are too small, and so on. So we can actually control the size of the fragments and the way that we do that is my machining grooves on the inside. And the reason we do that is because when the detonation wave is actually running around the inside of the body, it will actually reflect from these -- part of the wave will actually reflect from that groove and so that that will magnify the force acting on the shell body at that point and it will actually fracture along those -- along those control surfaces. What may have happened is that during the manufacturing process then there could have been a small defect at that particular point. We would have had a reflection from the shell body of part of the detonation wave that would magnify at that place. We would have preferential failure on one side of the shell body rather than the other. That would then vent the gases more from one side than the other, and so that would cause the -- the tail fin to actually rotate about its centre of gravity and to actually cause it to yaw. That's one particular possibility. I find that difficult to believe as well because the -- they're normally inspected very, very carefully, because if you do -- one of the reasons we don't use notches very often in practice is because they can trap air and TNT, which is the explosive used for this, TNT is actually cast, and so we can get air entrapped within the TNT because of these grooves and you get adiabatic heating due to the compression of those air bubbles and you can get in-bore explosions, which again is not very popular. So we tend to avoid that and normally pay very close attention to any defects that may be in the body of the shell because of that. The only other conclusion I can come to is that if it was a forging, then it would have been heat treated in order to obtain the correct properties of the shell body. And a heat treatment processes, they are notoriously difficult to control and it could have been an uneven heat treatment which had caused it to burst on one side before the other. And I think that's probably the most -- the most logical reason for that. But whatever did it, then it would cause an asymmetric force acting upon that fin and would have caused it to yaw immediately had that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now go to page 8. It is from that point of view that I am interested in the following: To what extent can this impact on the axial position of the stabilising boom, i.e., to what extent can this influence the way the angle is measured? I apologise, it must be page 7, and we will look at page 8 later. Page 7 where we see a drawing.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Can I just read the text so that I can understand the question more easily. Okay. I think what you're asking is how does this affect the angle of the -- the axial angle of the tail boom in the ground. Well, clearly if the -- if you have an asymmetric force acting on the projectile causing it to rotate it about its centre of gravity, then what will happen is that the impact angle will be different to the trajectory angle and -- but that will be by -- it will vary by an unknown amount because we don't know the extent of the symmetry of the force and the effect it will actually have on the rotation, it could be great or it could be small.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now let's talk about the specific case. Were you in a position to make a conclusion about the angle, i.e., whether the angle of the tail boom which was embedded in the crater at Markale was the correct indicator of the impact angle at the moment when the projectile touched the ground? What was your conclusion? Was it possible to arrive at the right conclusion with regard to the angle, first of all; and second of all with regard to the distance from which the projectile was fired?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: In answer to your first question about the angle of impact, then there are other factors at work here in addition to the axial rotation due to this asymmetric force acting upon the tail boom due to the -- due to the explosive charge. There is the -- the question that at the beginning of me giving evidence, then I described how we need to get the geometry of our projectile correct in order to ensure it's stable; in other words, we have to get our centre of pressure behind the centre of gravity. What we now have, we have a projectile consisting of just the part of the tail boom, not even all of the tail boom, just part of the tail boom. And so we have a projectile which is a completely different configuration to the one that we were first considering. So we still have stabilising fins, but now we've lost all of this mass at the front so that we've lost -- so that means the centre of gravity has drastically moved rearwards, but so has the centre of pressure because the centre of pressure is not just made up of the forces acting on the tail fins there, it's also made up from the forces acting on the front of the projectile, on that front diameter, on that nose part, and so we've lost that. So that in other words, what we've got is we've got the movement rearwards of the centre of pressure and we've also got the movement rearwards of the centre of gravity. What we do have now is the situation where the centre of gravity and the centre of pressure are much, much closer together so that I think looking at it, you probably have to do the sums, but it looks as if it would probably still be stable, inasmuch that the centre of pressure is still probably just about behind the centre of gravity. But it does mean that very small changes in that centre of pressure can have quite a large effect on the rotation of the tail boom about its centre of gravity. What we have to remember is that when this continues its flight from the moment that it's separated from the main body of the bomb, that main body disintegrates, moves out radially. This then flies through the remnants of the explosion. Now, those remnants will be there -- if we look at the -- a typical pressure time curve, what will happen is that the pressure inside the shell body rises almost instantaneously, not quite instantaneously, but almost instantaneously. The detonation wave actually moves at a velocity of about 6.9 kilometres per second, so that what we're getting is that we're getting a pretty sharp rise in pressure to a very, very high level. Then once the detonation waves pass and we've converted all of our explosive behind it into an explosive gas, that will then start to expand and the pressure will start to decay. But the -- those gases will be expanding at very, very high velocity. We're talking of kilometres -- many kilometres per second, and so that they will be flowing over the -- over this tail fin as it's passing through the air. You've got an asymmetric nose on it now, so that will develop lift and push it about its centre of gravity. Now, what can happen is that that can -- that could actually push it back and actually correct for the movement or it could actually add to it, so that you can see you've got a lot of things going on there. And so that the final velocity when it -- the final angle, I beg your pardon, when it hits the ground, then that will be very -- that will vary from round-to-round fire. And for this particular one, then it will depend upon the direction of those two forces. The first one that destabilise -- that actually started to rotate due to the asymmetric force and the other one due to the lift which is actually being generated due to the high-velocity gases flowing over it and the relative magnitude of those forces. So if the rotation -- if the original rotation was small compared to the other one, then you might get no interaction between them. You can see that it's impossible to actually quantify that, those values. That's why I say, it's really impossible to actually say whether, in fact, the tail boom is actually aligned with the actual trajectory -- the impact trajectory.

So that we have a fuse trough, but that's partially masked by the fact that the fins are 120-millimetre wide, they're the same diameter as the projectile, whereas the fuse would have been smaller, although upon impact and also due to the explosion, then you would have expected the fuse to -- components would break up, could be broken from the actual fuse body itself, and you would expect the fuse to be distorted and it could in fact be flattened and so that the actual diameter as a whole may in fact be greater than the original diameter of the fuse. Now why I would expect it to be like that is because for the last two years I have actually been firing trials where I've been firing projectiles into the ground at these sort of velocities, and the reason I've been doing that is I've been looking to develop disrupters for disrupting improvised explosive devices which are actually buried in the ground, and I've also been firing something which is significantly bigger than this and looking at using a gun as a pile driver for driving piles into the ground. And one of the things I've noticed is that even for quite small projectiles travelling a relatively small distance through the soil, then because of the material that they're actually passing through, then you end up with considerable abrasion -- abrasive marks, especially on the points, especially on this area here where that's forcing itself through the ground, and there are none -- none at all on this tail fin. You've got some abrasive marks on here, on the fins, as shown in the photograph. And so that's how I came to the conclusion that something very similar to this must have actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Allsop, what is the significance of the composition of the soil? What effect does it have to the determination of the angle of impact and to the position of the tail boom itself?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: The composition of the soil would have affected the actual depth of the penetration of the -- of the fin. If we consider if there had been no preformed hole in the ground that the tail boom entered into, then it would have gone through different layers of soil, different types of soil. The reports that I have read tell us that it would have gone -- that we had asphalt to start off with, and then we have the -- a layer of sand and gravel, sand and gravel are particularly abrasive. I'm not sure if there was a third layer from the reports, and I'm not sure whether in fact the soil in that area was in fact sand and gravel or whether there was a layer of sand and gravel that was laid down underneath the asphalt. That's unclear from what I've seen. But it is, nevertheless, it's a multi-layer of different materials. And any method trying to calculate the depth of penetration for different velocities would be very, very difficult. I have to do it for all the trials that I'm doing, and there I'm -- I deliberately use different types of soil all the same different types so that I'm -- I'm trying to simulate penetration into pure sand, pure gravel, a mixture of the two, but I make sure that they're all homogeneous. And I'm having great difficulty even under those circumstances in tying up the relationship between penetration depth and the impact velocity for these different soils. What I have found as well is that - and the literature tells us this - that the depth of penetration is significantly affected by two other factors, and that is it's affected by the moisture content of the soil. The thing which is the largest -- has the largest effect on the depth of penetration is the friction, is the friction between the projectile and the soil itself. And to actually reduce that friction, then we can do a number of things. But one of the most important ones is the soil content because water acts as a lubricant. And, in fact, you notice that the civil engineering industry, when it's piling -- when it's pushing piles into the ground, the resistance to those piles is mostly the -- due to the friction. So what they do is that they water the area and that significantly reduces the resistance to the piles. The other thing is the yaw angle, because what's happening is if the projectile has any yaw at all - in other words, if the angle is -- of the projectile is different to the angle of the trajectory - then we have the sides of the projectile which is now in greater contact with the soil, and so we again have a significant effect upon the penetration depth. And you only have to go for 2 or 3 degrees, it's very little, and it has a massive effect on the penetration. I was amazed just how big that effect is. So in my conclusion I find it very difficult -- it would be almost impossible to predict from the depth of the mortar what the impact velocity of the projectile -- of the tail boom would have actually have been because of these different factors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Allsop. When the stabiliser is taken out and then re-inserted, did this have any additional effect? Given what you have said, it seems that it's difficult to draw any conclusions even when the stabiliser isn't moved. If the stabiliser boom is taken out and then re-inserted, in what way does this affect the possibility one has of drawing relevant conclusions?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: The hole made by the -- both the fuse and the -- and then modified by the tail boom, the fins on the tail boom, that is through a material which has very little cohesive strength. And so that the removal -- actually, when you removed it, the tail boom, from the hole, then it is almost certain that you would have had sand and gravel which would have actually have been dislodged from the walls of the hole and which would have then fallen into the bottom of the hole. The fact that it was possible to re-insert the tail boom to the same depth, especially when you actually then go to push it back in, you're going to disturb even more soil, so you would expect therefore the hole to be at a less -- the hole to be not as deep as it originally was due to this additional material which is now in the hole. But from the video that I've seen of before and after, it seems as if it was -- the tail boom was actually inserted to a very similar depth in a similar position. So I can -- again, that's what leads me to believe that, in fact, the fuse was at greater depth than the tail boom so that it could actually accommodate this extra material which must have been dislodged. Anybody that's had anything to do with removing a rod of any sort from the soil will know that the hole tends to fill up from the material dislodged from the walls of it. As I say, I've been firing trials into different materials over the last two years, and it's very, very apparent on some occasions then just through removal of the projectile almost completely fills the hole, and I would find it almost impossible to actually push it back into its original position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for the witness at this point in time, Your Excellencies. Could I tender this statement into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. This will be admitted as next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 1D5015 will be Exhibit D2372.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gaynor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Hello, Dr. Allsop. We -- we'll be speaking the same language here and the interpreters are simultaneously translating what we're saying to each other. Added to that, some of the terminology both of us will be using is relatively unfamiliar, so I think all things considered we can afford to go fairly slowly.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Allsop, I just want to confirm with you that you agreed to meet two of my colleagues and me on Monday in the presence of Mr. Robinson for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes, I confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's right. Now, thank you for attending that meeting. At that meeting you referred to a document which had been provided to the Defence by the Prosecution which had been drafted by Dr. Berko Zecevic in which he made some observations about your report; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I'll be asking you a few questions about your report, about your testimony today, and about some of the figures which appear in Dr. Zecevic's report. First of all, I'd like to clarify the nature of your expertise. It appears from your CV, that's D2369, that you do have considerable experience in small arms; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, you've listed in your CV a total of 44 items of research and consultancy work. Now, in those 44 entries we see a reference to mortars in one of them, that's number 24, which refers to an 82-millimetre mortar. Would it be fair to say that mortars have not formed the central part of your professional career?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: That is correct. I should point out that I have, in fact, carried out considerably more work than in my CV. What I've tried to do is draw on the main parts of where I've actually concentrated my efforts over the years, purely because those are the larger contracts that I've actually worked on. But I've actually provided considerable assistance to our firing range. We have our own firing range down on Salisbury Plain in which we carry out trials, and part of my duties was to advise on the setting up of firing trials and actually carry out the analysis of such -- or advise on how to carry out the analysis on many of those trials. And many of those trials actually covered the fragmentation analysis of different mortars. I've actually been working on -- if you notice the -- on that last page of my CV, then I've been working on the 60-millimetre mortar, and what that consists of is that the UK has recently introduced a 60-millimetre mortar into service but it has no training rounds, so that I've been doing all of the analysis of the ballistics of the 60-millimetre mortar in order to design and produce a training round, an inert training round.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Okay. Is it fair to say that you did not have familiarity with the 120-millimetre mortar system used by the Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: That is correct, I didn't -- I didn't have familiarisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I just want to ask you a couple of questions following up on what you said about firing ranges. Now, the main purpose of the 120-millimetre mortar is to kill personnel in the open?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: It's not predominantly used to destroy buildings, for example?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Predominantly no. In fact, they have produced -- and I believe they have with the 120-millimetre, the latest barometric warhead which, in fact, produces -- enhances the blast. They mix aluminium with the explosive and this increases the impulse, and it's used specifically for destroying buildings and so -- so that I don't know whether it's available in the 120-millimetre. I know it's available in the 182-millimetre because I did the trials on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we'll come back to firing ranges a little bit later on. For the moment I want to address two questions that we discussed on Monday. The first is a theory concerning the Markale I incident. Now, the Judges have heard a witness refer to a theory that that incident was caused by a roof-top delivery of a 120-millimetre projectile from a building of five or more storeys into the market-place down below. Do you accept that theory?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you explain why you do not?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: There are a number of reasons. The first reason is that all of these projectiles, then they have a fuse for a very good reason. One is, of course, to initiate the explosive when it impacts the target, but an important feature is for it to be safe in storage and so that the -- when the projectile is actually -- before it's fired, if you dropped it, it would not initiate it because the fuse prevents it from doing so. And so that when the projectile is fired, it arms the fuse and it does this by the setback forces. The acceleration is thousands of G, you know, so that the actual setback forces on the fuse is extremely high. And so it's those setback fuses that actually arm the fuse. And you have to somehow -- if you had a conventional -- if you just had a 120-millimetre mortar bomb, then you would have to find some way -- if you were going to drop it from a building, you would have to have some way of arming the fuse. And the -- just -- I think you might be able to do it if you hit the back of it with a sledge hammer, but if you did that, that might mark the back of the fins and you would see that on the subsequent fin. So that's one of the reasons. The other reason is no matter how you threw it, if you threw it, dropped it, or whatever, it would almost certainly drop vertically, and so that means the pattern on the ground of the fragments would, in fact, be almost perfectly symmetrical. Although it's actually difficult to see the fragmentation pattern of the 120-millimetre mortar on the ground, the one that was actually fired, it does actually show that, in fact, it was -- it did impact at an angle. So those are my main reasons for discounting that theory.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Just pausing for a moment for the interpreters there. Now, you know that a 120-millimetre mortar projectile weighs a little over 12 kilogrammes?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in the scenario that's been raised before the Court, the projectile was thrown from the top of a building of about 15 and a half metres in height so that it landed on the ground a minimum distance of 11.1 metres away from the base of that building I've just described. Do you accept that as a likely trajectory, if I may say so, or a likely scenario for the Markale I incident?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: No, no. I -- as I explained at our meeting, then I don't think it would be physically possible to throw a 12 and a half kilogramme projectile 11 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: It's further been suggested that someone ran out after the explosion in the midst of the dead and dying victims and plugged the stabiliser into the ground before the arrival of UNPROFOR officials or any Bosnian police officials. Do you accept that this is a possible scenario?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I find that highly unlikely. I've already been talking about the fuse trough and this actually entering into a preformed hole formed by a -- a fuse falling directly behind the fuse. The appearance in the video then -- that's exactly what I would expect, that it has all of the characteristics of a 120-millimetre mortar bomb strike.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, it's further been suggested that the Markale I incident might have been a static explosion, that it occurred on the ground. The citation for that is page 12357. Dr. Allsop, do you accept the possibility that -- or do you accept that it's a likely explanation that this was a static explosion?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I would not accept it as a likely one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you accept it's even possible?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Possible? I -- for the same reasons, one, you've got to arm this. How did the fin actually get into the hole? The only way that the fin could have got into the hole is because it was actually moving through the air at a higher velocity -- the projectile was moving through the air at a higher velocity than the ejection velocity of the tail fin. So I cannot see how the tail fin would have ended up in the hole from a static explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Right. And I'll raise one final scenario for your consideration, and that is the possibility of a 120-millimetre mortar projectile being buried under the surface of the asphalt. Do you accept that is in any way a likely scenario?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: That's not possible. You would not have had that characteristic. The asphalt's hardly been disturbed. You would expect quite a massive -- quite a massive crater formed by such an explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: All right. Now, Dr. Allsop, I want to change the subject slightly to a comment that you made and it concerns the safe use of mortar systems. And the point of -- when I say "safe," I mean safe for the crew which is firing the mortar. You said at page 13 today: "The way that we go to shorter ranges is by actually reducing the velocity, by going to a different charge system." Now, you were talking about the scenario of a very high trajectory --

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: -- at a very short distance from the intended target, where there's a possibility that the wind will blow the round back and it will land on your mortar crew?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can you just explain to Their Honours, perhaps, a little more about that. If you are relatively close to the intended target, is it at all wise to use a high number of charges?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Just explain a little further why that is.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Because you would have to -- if you're close -- if you're close to the target and you're -- you launch it with a large number of charges - in other words, at high, high velocity - it means that you've got to launch it at a very steep angle in order to achieve that short range. And so that there are -- you have two problems with that. The first, of course, to do with the possible danger to the crew because the projectile is going to be in the air for a considerable length of time, and therefore has the -- any -- providing wind acting on it for a long time. I've also explained that when you get up to the steep angles, small variations in angle actually has quite a large effect upon the range. And so consequently, you have to be very, very certain that you've got the thing aimed at the correct angle to actually ensure you're going to hit the target.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I want to move on to an assertion you make at paragraph 5.3 on page 3 of your statement, and it was an issue which was taken up by Judge Morrison and I'd like to ask a few more questions about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before that. Doctor, do you have your report in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to have one in hard copy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have one in hard copy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- in my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, you may consult your report at any time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I'll use the one on the screen for now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Just the -- I'm basically referring to the entirety of paragraph 5.3 in which you explain the essential relationship between the velocity at which the stabilising tail boom penetrated into the earth in comparison to the ejection velocity. And you've explained it very well there at paragraph 5.3. And I want to just ask you a few questions about some ideas which flow from that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, first of all, you confirm that that paragraph applies to the situation at the Markale I incident site?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, the rearward velocity or the ejection velocity, as you wish, will be the same regardless of the impact velocity of the projectile; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: The impact -- I would put it this way: The impact velocity would not affect the ejection velocity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Although it, as I've already tried to explain, then there is a variation from round to round in all of these things, in the launch velocities, in the rearward ejection velocity, and so on. And so when you say it would be the same, it would be -- that's why I put it in those terms --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: -- that the impact velocity does not affect the ejection velocity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Right. I've noticed that you rely a great deal on extreme levels of precision - and that's not a criticism. When I say "the same," I mean roughly the same.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, just moving on. The density of the surface on which the detonates does not affect the rearward ejection velocity, does it?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The angle of the projectile, the point of impact, it does not affect the ejection velocity either, does it?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I would like to consider three scenarios --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Slow down, please. Put a pause between the question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you for that reminder, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'm now going to turn to three scenarios. In the first scenario the impact velocity is greater than the ejection velocity, so the stabilising tail boom will be driven forth, towards the surface; correct?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In the second scenario, the impact velocity is about the same as the ejection velocity, so the tail boom will be retrieved in the general vicinity of the impact point?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And the third scenario, the impact velocity is considerably less than the ejection velocity, so the tail boom might be found a considerable distance, you mentioned 250 metres, from the impact site?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, it follows that in the first scenario the impact velocity is greater than the impact velocity in the second scenario, which is in turn greater than the impact velocity in the third scenario?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd now like you to consider the question of charges. The Trial Chamber has received evidence that this was a 120-millimetre M62P3 mortar projectile. Now, we can bring up, please, 65 ter 23723B. Dr. Allsop, this is an extract from the firing tables for the -- for this family of 120-millimetre mortars, the M74, 122-millimetre [sic] mortar. I'd just like to draw your attention to the first two sentences of paragraph 56 which appear on the right-hand side of that. If you could read those, please. Now, can we confirm that this system is not designed to be fired with zero charges?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Some mortar systems can be fired with zero charges, can't they?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Most of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: But this particular one, no?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: From that, that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. Now, there are six possible charges which can be used with this particular mortar system; do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. Now, the velocity for -- the velocity at the moment of firing increases depending on how many charges you have on it; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The more charges, the higher the firing velocity?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, perhaps I can tender that at this stage, Mr. President? It's part of the firing tables. It's simply to confirm that it cannot be fired on zero charges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this will be admitted as next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P5946, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd now like to turn to the relationship between firing velocity and impact velocity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, again I'm going to invite you to consider three scenarios, and in this situation I would like you to assume that the firing location and the impact location are at the same altitude.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd also like you to assume that the angle of impact in each of these three scenarios is identical.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: You say the impact, not the launch?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The angle of impact, correct, yes. The angle of descent at the moment of detonation, if you like.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: The angle of descent is the same, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. Now, in the first scenario --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Sorry to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wanted to put this question at the last moment, but it -- because this was raised. We heard two times. On my part I'm confused about it. We heard "angle of descent" and "angle of impact." Are they referring to the same thing or are they a different notion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They are the same?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. -- I'm sorry. So then you also mentioned, Dr. Allsop, the angle of projectile and angle of trajectory.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That -- is that similar -- identical to angle of impact or angle of descent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The -- what happens is that when we launch a projectile into the air, it will follow a trajectory. The check -- the definition of the trajectory is the line traced out by the centre of gravity of the projectile through the air. So that means that the angle of the trajectory is always changing. So it will start off with, say, for instance, approximately 45 degrees in this direction and end up at 45 degrees in that direction, so you can see it's always changing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the last angle of trajectory is identical to the angle of impact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The -- that's correct. But the angle of the projectile does not necessarily match the angle of the trajectory. Under such circumstances it's because the projectile is yawing.
