It's the -- the projectile is designed so that it should -- the angle of the projectile should follow the angle of the trajectory. But under certain circumstances, then it will not, so that means that it will actually be yawing, the angle will be different. So then consequently it will be yawing and the stabilisation system will eventually push it back so that you will actually be following the same angle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Yes, Mr. Gaynor, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Going back to the three situations -- the scenario I raised earlier. I'd like you to consider where the impact velocity of the projectile -- sorry. We were on the relationship between the firing velocity and the impact velocity. Could you give the Court an idea of the relationship between those two on a level playing field where the firing location and the impact location are level?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: The relationship between the launch angle and the impact angle?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No, the velocity --

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Okay, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Launch velocity and the impact velocity.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The launch velocity and the impact velocity, the relationship between those two.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: In the circumstances where there was no drag, they would be the same, no aerodynamic drag. If it was in a vacuum, it would be -- but the fact that it's actually passing through the air, it means there will be a loss in velocity. And -- but that loss is quite small because these projectiles are moving relatively slow compared to most military projectiles, and so that means the aerodynamic drag is relatively small. But they will be similar but always will be -- under these circumstances it will always be lower.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want you to consider just briefly - I'm sorry to take you through these, but I think it's vital for us all to follow - the first scenario, the impact velocity of the projectile is considerably less than the ejection velocity. Now, it's likely that this projectile was fired on a relatively low number of charges, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: So the impact velocity is -- could you -- I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The impact velocity is considerably less than the ejection velocity, so the tail boom is kicked back at -- a long way.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well -- that is -- I'm just going back to the equation that you gave us earlier, where the impact velocity is -- of the projectile -- or if you prefer of the tail boom --

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: -- at the moment of detonation is considerably less than the ejection velocity, then we're going to get a kick back?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: We're going to get a kick back, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Right. So the tail boom will be found, as you said, up to 250 metres?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes, we've agreed that part. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Right. Now, in that scenario it's likely, all things -- I'd like you to consider that this was fired on X number of charges, all right.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Fair enough. Now, let's move on to the second scenario. The impact velocity is about the same as the ejection velocity?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So as we said earlier, the tail boom will be found in the general vicinity of the impact location?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So it's likely to have been fired with a higher set of charges than the first scenario?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in the third scenario, the impact velocity is greater than the ejection velocity?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So the tail boom is driven into the ground?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: It's likely that in this scenario the stabiliser -- correction, the projectile was fired on an even higher set of charges than in the first or second scenarios?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, we must turn now to the influence of altitude on the impact velocity.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I want you -- I want to ask you about this. Do you accept as a general rule when you're firing a projectile from an elevated location towards a target which is located at a lower elevation, that the velocity is increased and indeed the range is increased than if you're firing at a target which is located at exactly the same elevation as the firing location?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I want you to consider a scenario where the land rises as you move away from the target. The land is rising -- I'm not suggesting it's rising uniformly, but it's rising into hills?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: It goes from 400 metres and carries on to about 700 metres, perhaps 6 kilometres away, so that around 7-, 750 metres. So around 6 kilometres away the firing location is around 700 metres higher than the impact location?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to go back to our three scenarios again, and again I would like you to assume that the angle of the projectile at the moment of impact in each of these three scenarios is identical.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Okay, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, on the first the impact velocity of the projectile is considerably less than the ejection velocity?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So it has been fired on X number of charges?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In the second, the impact velocity is about the same as the ejection velocity?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The tail boom is found in the general environment --

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: -- of the impact location?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: It's likely to have been fired on a higher set of charges than in the first scenario?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now in the third scenario, the impact velocity is greater than the ejection velocity.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The tail boom is driven into the ground.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: It's likely to have been fired on an even higher set of charges than the first scenario or the second scenario?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now let's just examine more closely the influence of altitude. If, for the sake of argument, you were to fire a projectile at a target located around 6 kilometres away at a charge 6, and you were located around 750 metres above the altitude of the target, the effect of altitude would be some acceleration and some greater range?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. Now, if you were to fire the projectile from much closer to the target where the altitude difference is less than the effect on acceleration and range would be less than in the first scenario I've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Okay. So that is to say the acceleration due to the difference in altitude would be more pronounced in the case of a projectile fired from 6 kilometres away than in the case of a projectile fired from a firing location closer to the target?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So I'm going to invite you to consider that assuming that the angle of a projectile at the moment of detonation is identical and you're firing on charges 1 through to 6 in the scenario I've just mentioned, for the tail fin to be embedded into the ground at the impact location, it is more likely that it was fired on a higher set of charges than on a medium set of charges or a low set of charges?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I'm not sure that's the case. I can see that -- I can see your argument leading up to this because what you're saying is that -- the thing which I'm having difficulty with is this high, medium, and low. In other words, what you're implying is that it will be charge 6, charge 3, and charge 1. I could imagine a set of circumstances where it would be charge 1, 2, and 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, let's take it that we at least agree that for the tail fin to be embedded in the ground, it must have been higher than for the tail fin to be found in the general vicinity of the impact location and in turn higher than for the tail fin to have been found 250 metres away?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Those impact velocities, yeah, that is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So we can agree on that essential scenario, can we?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes, there -- I have some concerns with -- you're using the words "likely" and you're using exact figures. The trouble is that ballistics isn't like this. In other words, your -- you have a range of ejection velocities. If you took your tail fin -- if you took the whole -- if you took ten mortar bombs onto a firing range and you fired it statically, though those ten, what you would find is you would have a range of ejection velocities. You have a dispersion. If you did a calculation and you sat down and you said: I'm now going to calculate what the ejection velocity was and it was possible to do that -- but nevertheless, let's assume it was possible to do that, you would come up with an ejection velocity of 200 metres per second. Theoretically, every one of those projectiles that you detonated would have an ejection velocity of 200 metres per second. That's not the case. If you carried out your test you would find that there is a dispersion of velocities, and that dispersion would have a standard deviation --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Okay. Can I just interrupt you there. We'll get on to ejection velocities in a second. Just give us a percentage indication of the approximate dispersion in the ejection velocity using, you know, fairly well-produced 120-millimetre mortar systems?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: That's the problem. We don't have that data. The only place that you can get that data is from firing trials and nobody's carried out those firing trials.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Right. Now, you accept that the former Yugoslavia had a highly advanced weapons manufacturing industry before the war?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: They had very advanced testing systems as well as factories?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, it's fairly likely, I put it to you, that one 120-millimetre mortar round produced by that industry is likely to have approximately the same performance properties as another round of the same model produced in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I'd -- this is where I would disagree with you because, in fact, in my experience I'm amazed -- you would say my experience is not of the former Yugoslavia-produced mortar bombs. Mine -- my experience is testing 81-millimetre mortars and 60-millimetre mortars and produced in Germany and produced in the UK. And what I'm always surprised about is the big variation in the performance of the fragmentation from the -- from round to round. And it's a major problem for me because I have to do the -- I actually have to do the lethality calculations afterwards. And so that I have to put these large tolerances on, which is not like the [indiscernible] by the analysis, but nevertheless they -- they are much greater than you would think they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'm -- just want to take you up on ejection velocity. In your evidence in chief at the end of page 20 you said if the ejection velocity of the tail fin is very low, for instance, on our 81-millimetre mortar, then the tail fin ejection velocity appears to be very low, you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I certainly do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And you went on to say that it's very rare that you find a tail fin near the site of 81-millimetre mortars?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, when you said the ejection velocity of the 81-millimetre system is low, are you -- what are you comparing that against?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: The other fragments which are actually produced. Basically when we test a munition, we test it -- we test it for fragment distribution, fragment size, and fragment velocity. And so we get a range of velocities. One of the -- one of the things which we notice is that the -- the fuse is normally ejected at reasonably high velocities, sort of --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sorry, when you --

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: -- hundreds of metres per second --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So when you were talking of ejection velocity in that scenario, you were talking ejection velocity of the shrapnel, not of the --

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: No, no, the tail fin.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: It's the tail fin. Well then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you -- do you happen to know whether the tail fin ejection velocity, which you describe as very low in the 81-millimetre mortar system, is higher in the 120-millimetre mortar system? Do you happen to know the answer to that?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that. I don't know what the ejection velocity is on the 120-millimetre mortar, but I know that the ejection velocity on the 81-millimetre mortar we're talking about between 40 or 50 metres per second.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you accept that the 120-millimetre mortar system's likely to have a higher ejection velocity?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: It is likely to have a higher ejection velocity than that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Right. Now, I'd like to move back to the question of firing ranges. You visited test firing site, I think you mentioned one in the UK.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Have you visited test firing sites in other countries?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Not in other countries. I've visited several test firing sites in the UK.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: These are military test firing sites?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Right. Now, is it fair to say that in order to safely test mortars and artillery, you need a very large piece of land in order that you don't hit anyone, hit any civilians?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes, we use Salisbury Plain.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Right. And these are other test firing sites or in locations where they are clearly warned to the public to stay away?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So you can bring a mortar crew there and you can fire around 3 or 4 kilometres and you're quite sure that nobody's going to be injured?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Right. Now these are -- these test firing sites are usually located in areas such as grasslands, hilly areas, boggy areas, that kind of environment; is that true?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: There that -- yes. There are exceptions to that. Salisbury Plain and then in certain areas where we actually do our firing is quite flat actually and it's quite well kept and it's -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, the 120-millimetre mortar system or any anti-personnel mortar system is not designed to be used in an urban environment, is it?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So when you're training your armed forces to fire these systems, you bring them to one of these firing ranges and you let them fire, then no doubt mortar crews are trained in crater inspection; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: No, they often -- they don't get the opportunity of seeing the crater.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, insofar as a mortar crew does get training in crater analysis, it would take place in this sort of soft surface environment; do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: If -- yes, but as I say, mortar crews wouldn't actually inspect the -- would not inspect the crater. The reason being that when they're firing high explosive rounds, then some of them do not go off, they're called blinds. And so what you have, you have an impact area, and they don't allow people in there to look at these things purely because of the danger of unexploded bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Okay. Well, do you accept that certain armed forces, including the Australian armed forces, the American, and I believe the British, do train personnel - possibly not the mortar crews - in the art of crater analysis?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: That's correct. That's almost certainly likely to be the -- the ammunition technical officers, the ATOs, the bomb disposal, and specialist people like that who have to go along and inspect incidents rather than being part of the army which is actually trained for using the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well, Doctor. You accept that this training takes place largely in a soft surface environment?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: It would be that type of range, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can I ask the Registrar please for 23960F.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, this is -- these some photographs taken from Eagle River Flats in 2007 by the United States army corps of engineers, I believe. Now, these are obviously photographs of soft surface craters, do you agree?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I would agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, they're fairly messy?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I would agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The shrapnel pattern is far less defined than you find in a hard surface environment?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I would have thought so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd just like to tender that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could I just mention that, in fact, what you see is blast damage here. You're -- being pedantic as you noticed. This is due to the blast damage. And in fact, you'd expect the fragment damage to be farther out from -- and this is what you would be more interested in. But nevertheless, because it is grassland, then it's very difficult to actually see the actual fragment impact area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: But for a different reason for from what you've said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. And I think we've agreed that the shrapnel pattern is much clearer in a hard surface impact than a soft service impact?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Right. Now if one were to take army personnel and to train them in fuse furrow analysis, it would take place in craters possibly looking a bit like this; do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I tender that, please, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P5947, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to turn now to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we take a break, now?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Any time Your Honours wish. I'm happy to break now, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, I was mistaken. Yes. We have 15 minutes more.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now I want to turn to some data that we discussed on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I ask the Registrar, please, to bring up 65 ter 23960D.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, this is taken from a 1955 American study entitled: "Fragmentation of Brandt 120-millimetre mortar ammunition." Are you familiar with the Brandt or Thompson Brandt 120-millimetre mortar system?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you accept - I can give you the facts, if you wish - do you accept that it is very similar in terms of the mass of the body without the stabiliser, the mass of the stabiliser, the mass of the TNT in it, the mass of the fuse, and the length of the body, it's very similar to the M62, 120-millimetre mortar system from the Yugoslavia arms industry?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: The general characteristics appear to be very similar, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very good. Now, at the bottom of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Perhaps we can zoom in on the bottom part which is coloured -- yes, that's perfect. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, just under the dotted red line we see Fuse Frags and it seems to say 127 pieces. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, this suggests that the fuse has fragmented upon or in the milliseconds or microseconds after detonation into 127 pieces?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, below that we see the tail fragments and of interest far to the right is the stabilising tail boom which appears to be intact. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I accept that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So the stabilising tail boom is perfectly intact and the fuse has been blown to smithereens, to use an Irish expression.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you observe that?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I tender that, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P5948, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now I'd like to take us to 65 ter 23960E.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This is test data from five test firings of the 120-millimetre Brandt mortar system. And if we again focus on the right-hand side where the red and the green are, we see there -- if you're having trouble reading it, let me know, Dr. Allsop, but we see the Fuse Frags total, and underneath we see the weight and -- that's in the left-hand column, and on the right we see the number. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in the first test firing there are 90 fuse fragments, in the second there are 82, in the third there are 88, in the fourth there are 127, and in the fifth there are 107 fuse fragments?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, below that we see the figure 1, 1, 1, 1, 1. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now perhaps the Registrar can just move to the left. And we see that those figures refer to the tail?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So in all five of these test firings, the tail is intact and the fuse has been fragmented in many pieces?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P5949, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, do you agree that as a general matter aluminium is softer than steel?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you agree as a general matter that an aluminium fuse is more likely to be broken into fragments upon impact than a steel fuse, for example?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: No, I would accept the opposite.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, perhaps -- you remember we did discuss this on Monday?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, is that what you told me on Monday?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: We were discussing this and I -- I explained that the aluminium is more malleable --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. Malleability may well be higher, but do you accept that steel is harder?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes, but hardness is not an issue as far as the ability to actually fragment. I would accept that the aluminium would be more likely to be distorted --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: -- but to actually break into fragments, you've only got to look at the work of Mott, which was about the same time as Gurney, and he explains that the size of the fragments and the amount of fragmentation is dependent upon the brittleness or the opposite, the ductility. Also on the relationship between stress and strain, which is the Young's modulus, so that the lower strung -- strain, Young's modulus, then the less likely is to fragment. The aluminium has got about one-fifth the size of a -- and so on. So that as far as fragmentation is concerned, then steel is probably likely to fragment more than aluminium.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's move from the general to the specific, and I want to just inform you that the Trial Chamber has received a file of photo documentation taken by a crime scene detective who visited the Markale I incident site, took remnants from that site, cleaned, in fact, the impact site, and took photographs of remnants which were taken from the area around the impact location.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Those, for the record, the photographs taken are P1709, higher definition versions of those photographs have been admitted as P1970.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to bring up a photograph which is based on one of the photographs which has been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So I'd like to call for 65 ter 23960C, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, you'll recall that we discussed this photograph on Monday?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, those markings, I think it's fair to say, were put there by Dr. Zecevic and not by you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, do you have any reason to doubt Dr. Zecevic's identification of what he appears to believe are remnants of the fuse?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I think that the tip of fuse, that's fairly self-evident. The -- yes, it looks logical, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, do you also accept that this -- we've already seen it in the American photograph, and you know for your experience in this field, I believe, but do you accept that this is merely a very small number of the total fragments which resulted from the detonation of the Markale I projectile?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you accept that you cannot see any intact fuse in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: That is correct. These were collected from the surface --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: -- or from under the surface?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: These were collected before removal of the --

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Fine, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: -- projectile is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But just for the record, this is part of what exhibit and page what?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This is the photograph of the remnants of the Markale I projectile appear in the photo book relating to the Markale I incident which has been admitted as P1709. Now, because that photo book, especially when displayed on e-court, is somewhat indistinct, we also tendered high-definition versions of these photos which the crime scene detective Sead Besic brought with him here to The Hague. Those were admitted as P1970.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I just checked the P1970 which consists of only nine pages, and I didn't see this photo, but if there's no objection from the Defence there's no difficulty admitting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't have any objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. President, you might be right. These probably appear in P1709 not P1970.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. This will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P5950, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, do you accept on the basis of this photograph - and I think you referred to it in your testimony earlier, I can bring it to you after the break - that it is at least possible if not very likely that the Markale I fuse fragmented into several pieces upon impact with the asphalt surface?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Perhaps we can break there for the moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll break for 45 minutes and resume at 10 past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.25 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll note for the record that the photograph which has been admitted as Exhibit P5950 is an annotated copy of the photograph which appears at page 16 in the B/C/S version of P1709.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Allsop, we were on the question of the fuse at the Markale I impact site. You're aware that several people personally inspected the interior of the hole which was created after the stabiliser was removed?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Are you -- would you agree that finding an intact fuse at the impact site would have been of some assistance to the investigative teams investigating this incident?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I wouldn't expect an intact fuse, but certainly large components of that fuse, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now could we call up please D2370.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This is the diagram which you marked during your evidence in chief. Now in this diagram you've marked an intact fuse; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I marked an intact fuse to show the extra components that I would expect on there and from which fragments would have been left at the top, if you see what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. Now, in your earlier evidence today you said: "If for some reason the fuse completely disintegrated and was dispersed somehow sideways so that it did not -- so that no part actually impacted directly in front of it, then -- and if the stabilising tail -- stabilising boom was actually found in the ground, it can only be because the forward velocity of the stabiliser boom at impact was actually greater than its ejection velocity." You recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes. In what context was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You said it earlier on during your evidence in chief.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Is that when we were discussing different scenarios?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: It was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would it be possible to show the part of that transcript to Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By -- can we use Sanction or can we use e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, it's page 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This was not in response to a question from me. It was in -- I believe we'll have a look at it. Do you see it in the middle at line 10.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I'm just looking at in what context. Here we said: Thank you. Why do we refer to that -- thank you. Why do we refer to that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask the witness to speak to the microphone. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It's where I'm leaning forward to see the screen. Unfortunately, wearing glasses I difficulty in actually seeing the screen without leaning forward. Can I just see if I can -- there, that's better.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Dr. Allsop, perhaps I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Take your time, Doctor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can answer the question after having read them all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm reading what leads up to this question because I'm trying to see in what context the question was asked. Okay. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, are you aware that in the Markale I incident there's been no evidence admitted so far that an intact fuse was recovered from the hole created?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I am aware of that. I'm not -- I wasn't aware that anybody'd searched for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, you had a look at the photograph before the break and you accepted the possibility, if not the likelihood, that the fuse in this incident disintegrated upon impact with the asphalt surface?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: By "disintegrated," you mean completely -- I accept it would have broken up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: It fragmented?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: It -- yes. I normally -- we normally refer to "fragmented" as the action of the explosive. What you're talking about here is the action of the impact. So that it broke up into parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes. And -- yes, I accept that it may have broken up in -- well, it obviously did break up into some component parts because apparently some of them were actually found on the surface.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And you accept that upon break up into those component parts and upon impact with the surface, those component parts would be likely to move in a lateral direction; that's what you alluded to in your earlier answer?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: A lateral --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Sideways --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: The other component parts that were --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The fragments of the fuse.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: The fragments of the fuse as opposed to those that were actually embedded in the ground?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, we don't know that there were any embedded in the ground, do we?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I think we're talking at cross-purposes here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. -- or Dr. Allsop, rather, on the basis of the photographs you've seen --

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: -- of the fragments of the Markale I fuse, do you accept that there was, in fact, no fuse furrow created in the Markale I incident?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: No, I think that it would appear that we had the fuse -- part of the fuse break up and was therefore dispersed on the surface, and that the remainder of the fuse was actually driven into the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Certainly there was no hole created by an intact fuse, was there?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: By a -- not by an intact fuse, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I would like to move to question of reference which has been made. You've said in paragraph 9.1 of your report that: "Investigators have mentioned that this produces a hole (known as the fuse trough or fuse furrow) that is often sufficiently intact in shape to allow the angle of impact and the heading of the mortar bomb to be calculated from the ovoidal shape of the mouth of the hole." You can check your report if you wish.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: It's common ground, I think, that several of the people who looked at the hole at the Markale incident have used terms like "fuse" "funnel" or "fuse furrow."

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's agreed. Now, I'm going to put it to you that the hole created in the Markale I incident was relatively well defined. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: It was fairly well defined because of the penetration of the boom -- stabilising boom into the ground, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, if we accept the speed of the penetration of the boom, do we accept that there was some compression of the material around which the boom was embedded?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes, because as it -- as it penetrates, that material's got to go to go somewhere, and so the only way is to actually move out radially and that would compress the soil radially, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And Their Honours have heard evidence from Dr. Zecevic who replaced the tail boom into that hole and from others who carried out fuse furrow methods on that hole. I'm simply letting you know that.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Okay, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to put it to you those who have used the term "fuse furrow" or "fuse tunnel" to refer to that hole were, in fact, referring to a hole which had been created by the impact of the stabiliser?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: In this instance that may well be the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to move at this stage to the question of asymmetric damage at the front end of the stabilising tail fin.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before going further I wanted to make this statement. For the record, the paragraph 9.1 referred to was the one appearing on page 7, not on page 8, because we have two 9.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, we can agree, I believe, that the front part of the tail boom shows damage which is of an asymmetric nature?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, you have concluded that -- I'm looking at paragraph 5.5 on page 4, and there you talk about the failed surfaces forming a point which is offset from the centre of the longitudinal axis, you're essentially talking about the asymmetric damage, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And then you say: "This can only be because the shear forces were asymmetric which would have caused the stabilising tail boom to rotate about its centre of gravity by an unknown amount." Is that still your evidence?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I put it to you that there are two potential causes for an uneven break in materials. First an uneven force is applied to the object, such as you have posited; or second, there is an uneven natural breaking point in the material itself so the force applied may be totally symmetric but that the object will break in an asymmetric fashion. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: The force the time of failure would have been symmetric, but the force acting on the tail boom goes beyond the force acting at that time. What will happen is that the failure would have been asymmetric; therefore, the gases flowing from the explosion -- explosive products, they would have been asymmetric, and so that the forces exerted on the tail boom would have also have been asymmetric.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, can I put it to you that in that answer and -- well, no, let's set aside that answer. Let's be reasonable here. In your report you have made these assertions about fairly difficult ballistic properties without citation to any academic articles or any testing data whatsoever. Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: That's fair to say, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And, in fact, in your entire report I believe you have referred to one item outside a number of exhibits and transcripts provided to you by the Defence and that one item is a thesis for a Ph.D. by a student acting under your supervision; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to move on to the question of the journey of the stabiliser from the moment of detonation until the moment it terminated its journey in the ground. Okay.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, that distance is approximately 50 centimetres. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes -- I'm sorry, I'm using to working in millimetres, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: 500 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in your report you refer to the potential effect of the remnants of the expanding gases during that trip?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, you've given us some helpful indication of the relationship between the velocity of the outward blast compared to the velocity of the projectile. I believe that today you referred to a speed of 6.9 kilometres per second --

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: That's the detonation wave.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's the detonation wave. Could you give us an idea -- a rough approximation of the speed of the shrapnel and gas moving outward just in those microseconds after detonation?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: The speed of the fragments from the shell body, they would have been between 1- and 2000 metres per second, typically -- well, those are the typical fragment velocities for this type of munition. And the gases themselves, then they are likely to be at least twice that, two or three times that, where they actually vent past and expand into the atmosphere.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So it's fair to say that the outward movement of the gas and shrapnel is very much higher than the inward movement of the projectile?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: It certainly is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, do you accept the basic contention that gas tends to expand in a uniform manner?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: We've had this argument before I think. What do you mean by "uniform manner"?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, just to bring everyone else up-to-date, on Monday during our meeting I took down those words and those were the words which you yourself said in your discussion to me. All other things being equal, gas expands in a uniform manner where there is a very high pressure environment, heading outwards to atmospheric pressure on all sides.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: In uniform what we have is that we have a pocket of gas and so that that would have -- that would have expanded out in a uniform manner inasmuch as that it would have been perfectly symmetrical about that -- about the centre of the actual gas ball itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You said perfectly symmetrical?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Perfectly symmetrical, there would be some modifications to that purely because at the moment that the -- that you -- at the moment that you have interruption by -- from fragments, et cetera, that gas -- we have this ball of gas and we have these -- we have the -- and we have -- which are expanding outwards, we have the fragments which are expanding outwards, obviously the fragments are getting farther and farther from the centre of the explosion, so that that will be perfectly spherical at that point. A point will be reached where the gasses will actually hit the surface of the ground in one instance and that will start modifying the actual gas flow, but it will be actually symmetrical, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The purpose of the tail fins on a stabiliser are to maintain stability of the projectile while it travels through the atmosphere?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So extrapolating slightly from that, the purpose of tail fins is to maintain stability while the object is passing through a cloud of gas?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to move to the question of the potential impact of moisture on the impact location. Now I think you pointed out, and I think it's common sense, that if one sticks a spade into soft soil, the spade will go in fairly easily?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If you stick a spade into very hard soil, it will be much harder?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: It will, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So there's no question that moisture plays a role --

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Now you're assuming that the hardness of the ground is due to the presence of moisture.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Thank you for that clarification. Now, you're aware that the Markale Market surface was asphalt?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Which is also known as Tarmac essentially?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: It is, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And that is a waterproof substance. Water will form in puddles on a flat Tarmac road, won't they?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: It will, but it also -- it will actually seep through the Tarmac as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly make a pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: It is essentially designed to be non-porous?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: It is, yes. It's designed to actually shed water off of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: There is no evidence, in fact, that it was a rainy day on the day of the event in question. I'm putting that to you. Do you have any reason to disbelieve that?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: No, I have no reason to disbelieve that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, I put it to you that the subsurface material probably did not have any moisture content which could have really affected these measurements to any great extent?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I find that very surprising. Water does not just get into soil from rain in the atmosphere. It gets into the soil from a variety of areas. It depends upon the level of the water table. And water also, because of its capillary action, will actually move sideways so that I would find -- I would be staggered if, in fact, the material underneath the Tarmac was actually dry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'll move on now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I would like the Registrar to bring up P1970, starting at page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We're going to look at some photographs of the Markale I impact location, both prior to its cleaning and after its cleaning and indeed prior to the -- putting up some chalk marks around the shrapnel damage. You'll see all that in a moment. Their Honours have received evidence about this. Essentially towards the top of this photograph, approximately where the horizontal metal bar meets the vertical metal bar is the impact location.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we could move to the next photograph, please. Could we move to -- if that was photograph 5, I'd like the one prior to the last photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, there we see the impact location again. As you can see, there hasn't been any cleanup and you can't even see the top of the stabiliser fin. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I agree with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Perhaps we could move one back again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now here we -- you can see the top of the stabiliser fin; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I agree with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Okay. Now perhaps we could look at some other photographs. I'd like to call up, please, 65 ter 23063 and go to photograph number 4. This was taken on the following day. You can see that chalk has been marked around the impact location; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I can see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can we have the next photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You see again that chalk has been marked around the impact location?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, if you see the upside down figure 18, that represents the azimuth that was measured at the site.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, as you're aware, Dr. Zecevic measured the angle of impact based on the stabiliser which he re-inserted into the hole on the day after the impact. You're aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, he measured it to be 60 degrees, and he himself adds a margin of error of 5 degrees to either side, which is to say from 55 to 65 degrees.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I know he quoted this 5 degrees and I don't know how he came to that figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In his evidence I think he used the word out of modesty, but in any event we can accept that it's a margin of error of 10 degrees. Do you accept that 55 to 65 is 10 degrees. We agree on that?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Well, I don't what that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, I'm simply asking you to confirm. The margin of error was from -- is 10 degrees, right?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that that was the -- that that was the -- that that was the error --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Right. I'll put it a different way. That is the margin of error which was applied by Dr. Zecevic and which Their Honours are -- have received in evidence. All right. I'm simply letting you know. Now, you referred in your earlier evidence to the minimum and maximum angles of fire. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: The 45 and 85 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very good, yeah. And could you give the Court an idea of the minimum and maximum angles of impact of this mortar system?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: That would be at approximately -- approximately 5 degrees more in both instances. That would probably be about 50 degrees and approaching 90 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, let's just talk about 90 degrees for a moment. In what kind of combat environment would a 90-degree impact angle occur?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: When you were firing at 85 degrees, then it would come down almost vertically.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Okay. Let's just have a think about the wisdom of that form of operation. Is it the kind of mortar attack that any sane mortar crew would undertake?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Because it's coming down at 90 degrees it doesn't mean it's coming down directly on top of you. It will actually have moved out and then be coming down at 90 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. And just so I'm clear on this myself: What's the distance between firing location and impact location in that scenario?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: You would -- most mortars are not used under any circumstance that will actually impact closer than 500 metres to the crew.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I think we discussed this a little earlier, but essentially because of the possible impact and wind, et cetera --

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: -- it would be incredibly unwise to use that [overlapping speakers] situation?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So let's go back to your minimum and maximum rational angles. We would start with 50 and what would you say is the top end?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Around 85.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Around 85 . So that's 35 degrees?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Zecevic in the evidence which he provided to the Chamber has included a margin of error of 10 degrees out of a possible range that you've identified of 35 degrees. So he's approaching a margin of error of around -- I'm trying to do the calculation. It's certainly around 33 per cent. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, that is a fairly generous margin of error; can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, if -- even if one were to accept any of the issues which you've raised in your report, I put it to you that the possible impact on the trajectory of the projectile caused by any of those issues during those 50 centimetres that it travelled at high speed before being lodged into the ground was more than adequately taken into account by a margin of error of over 33 per cent?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Can I just read what you've just said because I'd --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Please, take your time.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Right. Now, I want to ask you -- you might want to clarify one of the assertions you make in your report which is at paragraph 11.1. I'll read it out. You say: "There was very little evidence on which to base a forensic investigation into where the mortar was fired from." You recall that?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, we'll get to precision in a moment, but for the moment I just want to understand the nature of the forensic evidence that you had at your disposal before you reached that conclusion. Could you give the Court a brief description of what the Defence provided to you relating to the Markale I incident?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I don't think I've got a list -- they actually sent me a number of reports and transcripts from previous trials. I should have brought the list with me; I'm sorry I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you look into other documents which is cited in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be the one. Can I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's page 10 of your report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me just have a look. There were -- there was other material other than that that was sent me because the -- these -- yes. I received probably twice as many -- I think about twice as many reports and transcripts of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: All right. Now, I just want to clarify some other points. You have never visited the Markale Market yourself?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Since you were never there, you have, I presume, no basis for disputing the observations of those who were directly at the scene and who saw it firsthand?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Specifically the observations of those who saw the impact location and cleaned around it?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Those who inspected the hole prior to putting the stabiliser back in?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You did not participate in the gathering of any remnants from the site?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, you did not have the opportunity to visually inspect the buildings around the area --

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I did not --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: -- to assist you -- thank you -- in the determination of the impact?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So you accept that you've been provided by the Defence with a very partial view of the evidence relating to this incident? Or do you accept that -- maybe put it another way. Do you accept that you might not have been provided with all the evidence that the Trial Chamber has before it?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I accept I have not been provided with all the evidence, but whether there is any other evidence which is relevant I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, I put it to you that you're not particularly well-placed to state that there was very little evidence on which to base a forensic investigation into where the mortar was fired from?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: In the reports, then the reports concentrated on calculating the velocity of impact and the angle of impact, and the position from which the mortar was fired from was calculated from these two factors alone. And therefore I had all of the information on how they were determined.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. At this point I'll get to my final point in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I tender those photographs. They were taken -- they were provided to the Prosecution by Sead Besic and they are not already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we're going to object to that because of a lack of foundation through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see the point. This -- we are talking about 23063, page 4?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The picture we had --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: 23063, page 4, and the preceding couple of photographs which I showed to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. While the witness has been asked to make comments on these photographs but there has been no real provenance other than what Mr. Gaynor has indicated about the photographs, who took them and when they were taken, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Is the Defence disputing the authenticity of these photographs? Do I understand that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have no dispute with it. I have no way of knowing, actually, but I take the Prosecution's word that they are genuine photographs, but Mr. Besic was here and could have been asked if they were useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, the Defence is not challenging the authenticity of the document, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: So what then is the main thrust of your objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That there's no foundation for the -- for the photographs being admitted through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: No legal foundation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Right. The witness has not really been able to comment on these photographs with the knowledge of exactly where they're from or at what time they were taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: First of all, the witness -- I don't believe the witness is disputing or has in any way disputed that these are photographs of the Markale I incident site. These documents go directly to the assertions by the witness concerning the distance which the projectile travelled before impact, his assertions concerning the accuracy of the measurements which could be made at the incident site, his assertions concerning the depth to which the projectile -- the projectile's tail fin travelled before coming to rest, and they are also relevant - apart from their relevance to understanding his evidence - to assessing the credibility of the witness on these specific points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber thinks there's a basis to admit this picture, but could you identify the page numbers that were shown to the witness. There are five photos, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, just one moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this not the only one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told that page 4 and 5 --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's my understanding, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- were shown. They will be admitted as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P5951, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Dr. Allsop, I'd like to deal now with the question of accuracy of data, and you have quite properly emphasized many times in your testimony how important it is to have very accurate data. Now, I want you to consider for a moment a scenario where you and I are a mortar crew and we are coming under fire and we wish to return fire.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in order for us to return fire, we must know the precise location of the gun which is firing upon us. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: If you are returning fire, is the purpose of this in order to intimidate or to actually hit the target? It may be that you don't know where the -- in military terms, and quite often you don't know where the gun is being fired from, but fire is actually returned in the general direction to intimidate, to let the -- let the opposing side know you are there and that you're -- if they do actually find out where you are, to actually -- to actually engage you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. Now, let's consider a couple of the scenarios you've raised. Now, if we wish to hit a precise gun, then we must take all the relevant factors into account, including the angle of impact of, let's say, a crater that we're inspecting, including the possible speed of the projectile, including the weather conditions, you have to take all of that data into account very carefully, don't we?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can I just read that? So let's consider a couple of scenarios. If we wish to hit a precise gun, then we must take all of the relevant factors into account, including the angle of impact of let's say a crater that -- including the weather conditions --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Let me start again, Dr. Allsop. I want you to consider that you're analysing a crater with a view to returning fire at the gun which created that crater?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: You're going to shoot back?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. I want you to just consider that for a moment.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: With the aim of not harassing fire, but of obliterating that gun?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Then you must have incredibly precise data to figure out where that gun is?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now if you're trying to hit harassing fire within a hundred metre radius of that gun, then the data can afford to be a little less accurate. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: As I've already said, that the -- within a hundred metres, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'm not tying you to the figure of a hundred metres. What I mean is if you go from trying to hit a precise target located many kilometres away to hitting an area many kilometres away, the degree of precision of the data that you need to know goes down?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, if you're trying to hit not only the area around that gun but a much larger area, the precision of the data you need goes down much further?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, if you are trying to determine whether you have come under fire from a location which is over 2.800 metres away in approximate direction of fire or under 2.800 metres away, then again the amount of data you need is less. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now the translation has been completed. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency, a few questions. Could Dr. Allsop please have a look at photograph number 5. 9949, I believe, which is in the e-court system at the moment. Could he have another look at the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see that photograph, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: This is the one that's on the screen at the moment? Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at this butterfly, this drawing, would you have drawn the central line that represents the direction from which the shell came or would you have drawn it a little to the left or a little to the right?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: This one is very difficult because you can see that in an ideal world that this should be perfectly symmetrical, this shape, and so that that would then be very -- very, very straightforward to actually align the axis along the line of symmetry. Unfortunately, as I was saying earlier, the fragmentation pattern is more erratic than that. And you can see in this particular case that the person did this, then he did the correct thing, he chalked around the area surrounding those fragments, and you can see that there are actually gaps in the fragment pattern. So it's then a matter of judgement as to how you actually align that axis. I must admit that the person that did that probably has more experience at doing these things than me, and so that -- I don't really think that I could improve upon that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that to the left of this axis there's a wider area than to the other side, and if it were moved further to the left, less than 18 degrees of the azimuth, would this be erroneous?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: As I've already said that in an ideal world this would have been perfectly symmetrical, but it's not. I think that there's a degree of error. I think that the person who actually drew that was drawing upon his experience, and would probably say that that is where he thinks it is. And I think you could make an argument that there is some degree of area associated with that, but I don't think that I have the -- I have the expert knowledge in order to comment further on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a look at the previous photograph. Could we zoom in to the central part where we can see the stabilising boom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Allsop, what is your opinion of these pebbles or rocks that we can see between the fins? How'd they get there and when? What is your opinion? Or was this perhaps fastened in this manner? Were the fins perhaps fastened in this manner?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: The reports indicate that the actual surface was sand and gravel, so that I assume that those stones that you see come from the actual gravel and this is the sort of thing you'd expect. I expect the reason that they're between the fins in that manner is that during the penetration into the ground then they -- in order -- as it was penetrating, it probably deflected on -- to the part of least resistance and so that they would have probably ended up in that manner. They may have also -- or you may have some of them which have actually fallen in from the top of the -- because we know that this was actually covered with fine layers of -- fine layer of asphalt almost dust. And so consequently it could -- I just don't know. I can't offer any other explanation than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a look at a different photograph, 9947, a photograph we saw earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Allsop, would you agree that the soil in this photograph doesn't seem to be dry? One would sooner say that the soil was moist?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: It's actually very difficult to tell from the photograph by -- it does look as if it is moist.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Doctor, did you complete your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so. It does appear to be moist, but I am looking at a photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, your answer didn't -- wasn't fully reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You said it looks as if it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It looks as if then the surface is wet, but this is only an appearance that -- I'm commenting on an appearance in a photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, do you know when this picture was taken?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I believe it was the day after the incident, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Allsop, do we agree that this photograph was taken after the stabiliser boom was re-inserted?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic is formulating his questions in a somewhat leading fashion I suggest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
