utterances.text: In that case, Dr. Allsop, do you know when the stabiliser boom was removed and do you know when it was re-inserted into the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I can't -- I cannot tell from these photographs whether this was before or after. When I did my analysis, then I had a copy of the video, and what I did then I -- the video clearly showed the stabiliser boom in the ground, which was actually being uncovered from the asphalt. And then it clearly showed the stabiliser boom after it had been re-inserted. I didn't see on the video it being taken out or re-inserted. But from these photographs, I can't tell whether this was before or after.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have this photograph, just this part that shows the stabiliser boom, to the left part of the screen; and could we have photograph number 48 shown on the right part of the screen. Could we have the next photograph shown on the right part of the screen. Could we zoom in the photograph to the right, the central part of that photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, would you like us to rotate the picture on the right side?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That would be better. Then we can see whether there is any difference. By 180 degrees. Yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They appear to be the same picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. It looks different from that other perspective. Thank you. Dr. Allsop, may I ask you the following. If this photograph was taken on the following day and after the stabiliser boom had been removed and then re-inserted, in that case what would you say about these small rocks, what is their purpose, and how is it that they are in the position that they are in?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: There's no -- there is no reason whatsoever for re-inserting the pebbles between the fins. To me, they appear to be almost the same photograph. I can't see any difference -- I'm trying to actually -- I'm comparing different features and I can't see -- I can't see any real differences. Even to -- if we take the stone which is in the 4.00 position, you can see that that's actually lodged on the top and it seems to be the same stone. So it looks to me as though it's the same -- almost the same photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Allsop. Yes, you can see it's the same -- the perspective was different, but what I'm interested in is the following. If these rock appeared there after the stabiliser boom was re-inserted into the tunnel, well, what was the purpose of doing this? Does this help one when an analysis is being conducted or does it make that analysis more difficult?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I can't see the reason for doing it, to actually place the rocks back in exactly the same position, because the -- for instance, the one that I was referring to, the boom must have actually been placed in there and then the rock placed on top of it. Why I do that, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a look at P1970 and then photograph number 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before doing that, shall we add photo number 3 to the Exhibit P5951?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, no objection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be done.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Photograph number 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you have a look at this photograph, is your impression that the soil is wet? The date is the 5th of February.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Yes. On this lower right-hand quadrant, then that appears to be almost a mixture of water and soil there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were asked about trials at the firing range in Great Britain, trials conducted only with one type of soil or various types of soils used when these trials are conducted? I'm referring to page 62 of today's transcript.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: The firing trials that I carried out in the UK, then they were against a wide range of soils to see the effect on penetration because we were primarily looking at developing a disrupting device for buried, improvised explosive devices. And although it was going to be used in the current conflict in Afghanistan, it was also going to be used in a wider context than that. And so we wanted to actually look at soils other than those commonly encountered in Afghanistan. So we looked at loam, sand, gravel, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 66 mention was made of the possibility of the entire fuse having fragmented, of all the parts remaining on the surface. In such an event, what would the fuse tunnel look like and what would the surface of the stabiliser boom look like?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: If the fuse has completely disintegrated and was lying on the surface of the ground, then there would not be a fuse tunnel. And the surface of the stabiliser, it really depends where the fragments whether -- as to whether they actually interacted with the -- with the stabiliser as it impacted the ground. So I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a look at P947 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you check the number again, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it is a photo, 5947, a photo of an area or some grounds in the UK. P947, P947 [as interpreted]. [In English] P5, P5, P5947. [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Allsop, look at the photo and tell us something about the sticks that you can see here. What do they mark? What do they denote?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Typically these would be used as reference points. The one with the red top on it, that appears -- the -- that appears to be close to the fuse funnel. And I -- typically I think that that would be used to actually align -- a rod to actually measure the actual angle of the fuse funnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about impact angle, would a stick or a rod point to that as well?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I'm assuming that in this photograph that a rod or a stick could actually be aligned with the fuse funnel and somehow marked on this stick in order to calculate the angle of impact of the projectile. But these -- I don't think these were actually fired in the UK, were they? I these were actually fired in America.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, these are photographs from Eagle River Flats in the United States.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, in any case it seems that the impact or the angle of the impact was almost vertical; right?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Looking at the actual shape of the impact crater, I would assume that the -- it's actually aligned as we -- slightly to the left, a line probably pointing at 11.00, and it looks as if it was actually an impact that -- actually a fairly shallow angle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When it comes to mortars and other weapons for indirect fire, can they produce horizontal fire? Can they fire a horizontal projectile?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: If you fire the projectile horizontally, then you would have nothing to absorb the recoil. And I should imagine that the mortar would actually recoil back very violently. The other thing with a 120-millimetre mortar, then it does have a -- it can be fired with a lanyard so that you can actually drop the mortar bomb down the barrel and it won't fire, and then you can actually fire it with a firing mechanism. You can use that fixed firing pin so that when it drops down, it is -- then the fixed firing pin actually fires the mortar. And typically in the UK we always use the type with a fixed firing pin, so you couldn't do that with a fixed firing pin but you can with a lanyard. You could actually fire horizontally. I've actually used a 51-millimetre mortar for actually firing 51-millimetre projectiles in an indoor firing range because we were doing some impact trials, but the recoil was horrendous.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Allsop, if the shell that fell on Markale had been fired from a distance of 4 kilometres, where would you expect the apex of that trajectory to have been?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: The apex of the trajectory is usually just beyond the midpoint. I would have expected it to be something like 2.2 kilometres, that order, 2.2, 2.3 kilometres from the firing point for -- over the distance of 4 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what about height of that apex? Where would you expect that to be?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: If we're firing at -- it really depends upon which charge we're using and at what angle we're actually firing it. So that if we were on top charge but firing at high angle, then typically the maximum height that a projectile can be fired is normally about 80 per cent of its maximum range. So if we were firing at very high angle, then the -- then the height of the apex would be 5 kilometres. These things go very high into the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you expect a shell that travels so far would also produce some sort of a noise, a sound?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Mortars are much quieter than artillery shells. The -- one of the reasons that the infantry did not like mortars is because they take them by surprise. They don't hear them coming, usually, and so they don't have time to take cover. The noise that you hear from an artillery shell is due to its rotation, very high rates of rotation, and you can hear them as they pass over you. On our firing ranges, then often they will fire from one side of the Salisbury Plain to the other and you will be doing trials in the middle, and so you hope that the gunner has got his calculations right. But the shells will be passing over the top of you to a -- probably at a height of 2 kilometres. And you can definitely hear them. But that's due to the rotation of the shell. And -- but mortars are -- once they're in the air, then they are very, very quiet. They have a very low drag, so that means that they have very little disturbance of the air, they're subsonic, so they don't produce a sonic boom, and because they come down steeply, as well, steep angles, they come down from a height and they are difficult to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it sometime happen that a stabilising boom with zero charge plus 1, that the surface burns and that there are the traces of that burn?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Objection, that's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does the temperature - and how often - leave the traces of burning on the surface of the stabilising boom and does the number of charges have an impact on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Objection, that's another leading question. Second, I'm not sure that this arises out of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I didn't follow what the second question was about. But in any event, could you reformulate your question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This has not been interpreted correctly. I said whether it happens and how often.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does the burning of the charge and how often, if it does, leave the traces of burning on the surface of the stabilising boom? I believe that my question is not leading. I don't know how else to formulate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you explain to us how it arises from the cross-examination of Mr. Gaynor?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, there was a reference to the traces, mechanical traces and others, on the surface of the stabilising boom. We were talking about the surface of the stabilising boom and that's why I'm interested in the traces and marks left by burning and whether the number of charges have -- has an impact on those traces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. President, there has not been any evidence given about traces of burning due to charges on the surface of the stabilising tail boom given today -- or certainly not in my cross-examination or I believe in the direct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did discuss traces, but those were mechanical traces, and now my question is whether the burning of the propellant leaves marks and traces as well. But it's up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will allow that question to be put. But do you remember the question, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only marks that are normally left on the stabilising boom actually comes from the primary charge. If we think that the boom, it actually has -- it's actually hollow, and you have the vent holes which are drilled into the side, and so that when the weapon is fired then the propellant burns inside the tail boom itself. They vent sideways to ignite the augmenting charges, but the hot-burning propellant, as it burns through those holes, then they tend to erode the surfaces. And if you actually look at the stabilise -- a photograph of the stabilising boom, you'll notice that the holes are actually oval and that's where they've actually been eroded by the propellant gases. Those are the only marks that you get from the propellant and -- on the tail boom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My last question, Dr. Allsop. From everything that you saw, from everything that you studied, and based on all that, can you conclude that it -- there is every reason to doubt that the Serbs had fired the shell that hit Markale in 1994?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think it is for the Doctor to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I seek leave to put to the witness one question which arises from the redirect?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And what's the question you'd like to put, Mr. Gaynor?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The question concerns the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not finish. If there is no answer to my previous question, then I intend to rephrase it, to reformulate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think that's the kind of question appropriate to be put to the witness, but that was the last question. Do you have any other question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would ask the witness whether today after having prepared his report and after having studied the case, whether he would still adhere to that report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. President, my question concerns the witness's identification of some water and soil he said on photograph next to -- could I ask the Registrar, please -- thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could I ask the Registrar, please, to bring up P1970, photo 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: While he's doing that, I'll remind you, Dr. Allsop, of what the evidence is. Dr. Karadzic asked you: "When you have a look at this photograph, is your impression that the soil is wet? The date is the 5th of February." Your answer was this: "Yes, on this lower right-hand quadrant and that appears to be almost a mixture of water and soil there." Now, Dr. Allsop, I simply want to put to you two sentences from the statement of the person who took this photograph and who cleaned that area. This is from P1966, the amalgamated witness statement of Sead Besic. At page 9, this is a transcript from a previous trial at this Tribunal, Dr. Allsop, the witness was asked: "You referred to trying to find the place where the projectile fell. Did you find that place?" The witness answered: "Yes, we did. We located it and we started to record the scene of the crime because the actual location there were -- there was lots of human tissue, lots of blood, a lot of items. I personally proceeded to clean this area so that we could see as much as possible the actual projectile and the way the projectile landed." My question to you is this: Is the area to the bottom right quadrant of the screen consistent with an area from which a lot of blood and human tissue has previous -- has recently been cleaned?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: I don't think I'm really able to answer that. It looks as if it has been cleaned, yes. But whether it's been cleaned from blood and tissue, I don't know, because they've been cleaned away.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Dr. Allsop.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gaynor. Yes, Judge Morrison has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Allsop, if I recall correctly, you said at one stage in your evidence that one of the areas that you've investigated as part of your professional work has been the issue of the lethality of rounds. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: And it's a slightly awkward noun, but we all know what it means. A lay view might be this, that the -- there is a radius of lethality which will depend upon the power of the explosion and the amount of fragments which are discharged above the ground. Is that a fair proposition?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: That's a fair proposition, but the blast has a much less range than the fragments. It's typically -- it's like 10:1 so that if you had a lethal radius, for instance, of 20 metres, you'd expect that the blast radius would only be lethal to about 2 metres and the fragment site at 20 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. And the lethality of a fragment will depend on its mass and its velocity presumably.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: And whether or not it's lethal given any particular target will depend upon whether, for instance, that person was wearing protective clothing or whereabouts on the -- his or her physique the actual -- the piece of shrapnel penetrated.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: That is correct. When we do the lethality studies, then what we do is we do it statistically, and so, for instance, the body is reckoned to have a lethal area of 17 per cent of its actual area. But although we talk about lethality, then what we're really looking at is incapacitation, not lethality itself, and in fact all of the studies are based towards incapacitation rather than lethality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: So the number of people who might be injured, if not killed, really depends on the number of people who are within the lethal radius of the shrapnel?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we adjourn, I have one further question, Doctor, I would like you to assist the Chamber again. You told us the angle of descent and angle of impact are the one and the same concept?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I'm of the impression -- but some witnesses are using those terms interchangeably but some witnesses seem to try to distinguish them. So can I show you one witness statement. Can we upload Exhibit P1276. This is a witness statement of Ekrem Suljevic who was a part of the MUP of Bosnia and who participated in the investigation of Markale I shelling. Page 4, paragraph 15. Yes. If you could read the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Paragraph 15?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. He says: "I am familiar with the concepts of direction of fire, angle of fire ... range ... angle of descent ... and the angle of impact ..." So -- but if you read the words -- phrases in the parenthesis, he explains the angle of descent as "the angle at which the projectile descends, which changes during the flight of the projectile," which is similar to the angle of projectile you explained to us earlier on.

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Again, he's talking about the same thing. The angle of descent is quite correct, that the angle of descent it will -- the projectile is fired into the air so that it is ascending. It will then -- it will then start descending so that that angle -- obviously it's horizontal at that stage. By the time it actually impacts onto the ground it's at the angle of impact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So at the moment of impact, angle of descent, angle of impact, angle of projectile, angle of trajectory, all should be the same?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: Should be the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, may I be allowed to put just one short question to the witness that arises from the questions of His Excellency Judge Morrison?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Allsop, when it comes to fatality, how would the obstacles impact the lethal properties of a certain weapon, do they increase it or decrease it?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: It really depends upon the -- upon what these are. If we take something like plywood, I'll say 10-millimetres' thickness, and you're fairly close to it, then this projectile would go straight through, it won't -- they'd -- it'd make a very little -- have a very little effect on their velocity and the direction. But what can happen is that they can actually produce secondary projectiles, and so that means that you can create lethal and injurious splinters so that you have a number of different effects, so that if you have something which is more robust they can actually stop, stop some of the projectiles. What we have to remember is we saw on one of the photographs that -- or one of the pictures that the Prosecution showed us and it showed to the distribution to the sizes of the fragments, and some of them are extremely small, they're very, very small indeed. In fact, they make up the majority of the fragments, and these are much more easily stopped but they -- by such things as, you know, 20-millimetre-thick plywood, for instance. And then we have some of the large projectiles, they would go a long way and they would do an awful lot of damage. They would actually -- some of them would pass through two or more people. In fact, we did some work on the -- a reconstruction of a suicide bomb which had 6-millimetre ball bearings and they were travelling at 1.800 metres per second, and they went through the equivalent of three people, and act at 25 metres. So you can see that it really depends upon the characteristics of the fragments and the actual -- and also the actual barriers to them. So I'm afraid all I've told you is that there are a lot of different -- a lot of different effects.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately the interpretation was not good. I was particularly interested in obstacles such as the stalls at the market. Did they increase or decrease the number of casualties?

utterances.speaker: DEREK ALLSOP
utterances.text: The stalls at the market, I would say that they probably decreased the number of lethal effects, purely because -- as I say that the majority of the fragments are, in fact, very small and are more easily stopped. Their velocity degradation is very high so they don't travel as far, so that as soon as you start getting much beyond by 5, 10 metres, then I think the stalls would have easily stopped those -- those small fragments. So the answer is they probably reduced the number of fatalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. That's it. And that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber I would like to thank you, Doctor, for your coming to The Hague to give it, and now you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But we all rise together. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 1st day of November, 2012, at 9.00 a.m.
